column4: This ayah directly calls night a “garment” (لِبَاسًا), making explicit the section’s shift from night spread over the world to a person entering clothing.
Night is made a garment, sleep a rest, and day a rising; the verse joins the section’s covering image to the night/day passage of the surah.
The section’s named root غ ش و appears as night covering its counterpart, an exact verbal scene for the night that envelops.
The section quotes people wrapping themselves in garments (يَسْتَغْشُونَ ثِيَابَهُمْ) to hide, while the ayah says God knows both what they conceal and disclose.
Nuh says his people put fingers in their ears and wrap themselves in garments (وَاسْتَغْشَوْا ثِيَابَهُمْ), an explicit act of clothing used to evade a warning.
The ayah names “the garment of taqwa” (لِبَاسُ التَّقْوَى) as better than bodily clothing, directly naming the section’s unseen protective layer.
God provides shirts that protect from heat and battle (سَرَابِيلَ تَقِيكُمُ), a bodily instance of the protective function the section reads within taqwa.
The criminals’ shirts are of tar (سَرَابِيلُهُم مِّن قَطِرَانٍ) as fire covers their faces, reversing clothing’s ordinary protection into part of punishment.
This ayah clothes the disputing unbelievers in garments of fire; the garment that should cover and protect instead belongs to the section’s warned-of fire.
Hell is their bed with coverings above them; this root-related covering is a punishment, the boundary opposite the protective cover in the section.
Canopies of fire above and below become an enclosing covering with no shelter, reversing the section’s image of a quiet protective layer.
The faces of those who earned evil are covered with pieces of dark night (أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ قِطَعًا مِنَ اللَّيْلِ); the same covering root becomes a sign of disgrace rather than shelter.
After the fall, Adam and his spouse begin fastening leaves from the Garden over themselves (مِن وَرَقِ الْجَنَّةِ); the scene makes clothing a response to exposure and loss.
The “wrapped one” (الْمُزَّمِّلُ) is addressed while clothed, but this address opens a call to rise for night worship rather than wrap oneself to evade a warning.
The “one who covers himself” (الْمُدَّثِّرُ) is directly addressed, echoing the section’s self-wrapping scene before the command that follows turns him outward.
“Your garments, purify” (وَثِيَابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ) connects clothing to purification, giving the section’s inwardly clean protective garment a concrete parallel.
The command to guard yourselves from the Fire (فَاتَّقُوا النَّارَ) makes taqwa a response to the very danger against which the section’s inner garment protects.
“Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire” (قُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا) states the safeguarding action named by the section’s root و ق ي.
The Lord protects the Garden’s people from the punishment of Hell (وَوَقَاهُمْ عَذَابَ الْجَحِيمِ), giving the protective root its final-fire setting.
This parallel promise also says God protects them from Hell’s punishment (وَوَقَاهُمْ عَذَابَ الْجَحِيمِ), linking taqwa’s safety to the section’s fire boundary.
Wealth and children are called the adornment of worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better; this distinguishes the showy mantle from what remains.
What people receive is “enjoyment of worldly life and its adornment,” while what is with God is better and more lasting, directly testing the section’s garment-as-ornament image.
Worldly life is described as play, adornment and boasting, then vegetation withers and crumbles; the scene makes visible the passing quality of the ornament worn by the self-sufficient.
Qarun comes before his people “in his adornment” (فِي زِينَتِهِ), staging the display of wealth that the section hears as a mantle carried on the shoulder.
The earth swallows Qarun and his house, and no group can help him; the adornment of the preceding scene offers no protection when it is time to fall.
The speaker says, “My wealth did not avail me” (مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ), almost exactly the section’s claim that wealth gives no gain at the moment of falling.
Abu Lahab’s wealth and earnings do not avail him (مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ وَمَا كَسَبَ), a direct counterpart to the section’s failed wealth.
The hoarder “thinks his wealth will make him live forever” (يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ), exposing the false security of wealth as a mantle.
The hoarded gold and silver are heated in Hell’s fire and brand foreheads, sides and backs; ornament becomes an instrument of exposure and punishment.
The human transgresses “because he sees himself self-sufficient” (أَن رَّآهُ اسْتَغْنَىٰ), matching the section’s miser who carries wealth as if it made him sufficient.
The sea overtakes Pharaoh’s people (فَغَشِيَهُم مِّنَ الْيَمِّ), using the section’s covering root for a fatal engulfing rather than a protective wrap.
The women are told to draw their head-coverings over their bosoms (بِخُمُرِهِنَّ عَلَىٰ جُيُوبِهِنَّ); this gives the section’s clothing image a bodily act of covering.
The women draw their outer garments close, with the stated result that they may be recognized and not harmed; clothing here has a protective social function.
Spouses are described as garments for one another (هُنَّ لِبَاسٌ لَّكُمْ وَأَنتُمْ لِبَاسٌ لَّهُنَّ), extending clothing from display to mutual closeness and covering.
This neighbour completes 73:1’s wrapped figure by telling him to rise during the night; the garmented stance leads to response, unlike wrapping to avoid admonition.
This neighbour completes the covered address in 74:1 with “rise and warn” (قُمْ فَأَنذِرْ), reversing clothing as a way of withdrawing from warning.
The command to guard against the Fire prepared for disbelievers repeats the section’s protective verb and places it at the boundary of punishment.
God protects the righteous from the evil of that Day (فَوَقَاهُمُ اللَّهُ شَرَّ ذَٰلِكَ الْيَوْمِ), a further instance of inward righteousness as safety.
The ayah calls taqwa the best provision (خَيْرَ الزَّادِ التَّقْوَىٰ); the section’s hidden garment can thus be read as what one carries for the way ahead.
The flesh and blood of sacrifice do not reach God, but taqwa does; this separates the unseen inward layer from visible material offering.
A structure founded on taqwa is better than one on a crumbling brink; the foundation gives another image of the quiet support the section assigns to protection.
The ayah lists gold, silver, livestock and fields among desires made attractive to people, giving specific material contents to the section’s adornment-like mantle.
This neighbour answers the desires listed in 3:14 with what is better for the God-fearing, completing the contrast between worldly adornment and inner taqwa.
Even silver roofs, stairs, doors and couches would be only worldly enjoyment, while the Hereafter is with the God-fearing; material ornament is bounded against taqwa.
After Qarun’s fall, the people who had wished for his position recognize that God expands and restricts provision; the neighbour interprets the failed display as no secure measure of worth.
This neighbour completes the self-sufficiency claim in 96:7 by saying the return is to the Lord, setting a limit on the wealth-backed confidence.
This neighbour to the failed wealth in 111:2 names the flaming Fire (نَارًا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ), bringing the consequence into the same wealth-and-fire sequence.
The verse condemns hoarding gold and silver instead of spending in God’s path, turning the section’s showy wealth toward the fire punishment described immediately after.
The warning not to let wealth or children distract from God’s remembrance connects material attachment to the section’s image of wrapping oneself away from a warning.

The source section’s dictionary branch gives “debt” as a sense of ridā; this ayah treats a debtor in hardship and urges respite, making that secondary debt-as-mantle sense concrete as an obligation one bears.
The ayah says God covers the day with night (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ), repeating the section’s root for night as an enveloping cover.
Here too the night covers the day (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ), another direct occurrence of the section’s night-covering root.
Night and day are repeatedly wrapped around one another (يُكَوِّرُ اللَّيْلَ عَلَى النَّهَارِ), extending the image from a garment to the alternating world.
David is taught to make armor that protects people from their own violence (لِتُحْصِنَكُم مِّن بَأْسِكُمْ), a direct bodily garment of protection.
David is told to make full coats of mail and then to do good; the ayah joins protective clothing with moral action, as the section joins garment and taqwa.
The earth puts on its adornment, its people think they control it, then it is cut down as if it had not flourished; this sharply stages ornament, false security and its disappearance.
What is on earth is made its adornment as a test of who does best in deed, making outward ornament answer to the inward measure of action.
People come to God alone and leave behind what they were given; this pictures the loss of worldly goods when the self stands exposed.
On the Day, wealth and children do not avail; this directly sharpens the section’s claim about wealth at the moment of downfall.
For those who disbelieve, neither wealth nor children will avail them against God, and they belong to the Fire; material support fails precisely at the section’s fire boundary.
The ayah repeats that wealth and children will not avail against God and places their owners among the Fire’s people, another direct reversal of wealth as supposed shelter.
The disbelievers will be unable to ward the Fire from their faces or backs; this states the limit of every bodily defense against the fire the section warns of.
The Fire’s pavilion surrounds its people, turning an enclosing cover into confinement and punishment rather than shelter.
The supplication asks God to protect its speakers from the punishment of the Fire (وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ), making taqwa’s protective root an explicit plea for safety.
Believers ask, “protect us from the punishment of the Fire” (وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ), matching the inner safeguard to the section’s fire scene.
The people of understanding likewise ask to be protected from the Fire (فَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ), a repeated formulation of the safeguard named in the section.
The angels ask God to protect the believers from evil deeds (وَقِهِمُ السَّيِّئَاتِ), extending the section’s protective root from bodily danger to moral harm.
God binds the believers to the word of taqwa (وَأَلْزَمَهُمْ كَلِمَةَ التَّقْوَىٰ) after placing tranquility in their hearts, locating the section’s protective quality inwardly.
The ayah says revering God’s signs comes from taqwa of hearts (مِن تَقْوَى الْقُلُوبِ), joining a visible practice to an inward layer.
This neighbour supplies the exception to 26:88: what avails is coming to God with a sound heart, setting inward condition against wealth and children.
God is the one who enriches and grants sufficiency (هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ), reversing the miser’s belief that his own wealth makes him self-sufficient.
This ayah completes the accumulation that distracts in 102:1 with its endpoint, “until you visit the graves”; worldly abundance ends at death.
The garden owner’s wealth is ruined, and he wrings his hands over what he spent; the failed property gives a concrete counterpart to wealth that cannot save its owner.
After the speaker says in 69:28 that his wealth did not avail him, this ayah adds that his authority is gone, completing the loss of worldly support.
The God-fearing are placed in a secure station (مَقَامٍ أَمِينٍ), directly linking taqwa to safety.
The people identified as God-fearing in 44:51 wear silk and brocade; this ayah places clothing within the secure reward of the protected, rather than the failed worldly mantle.
Night comes over Abraham (جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّيْلُ) as he observes the star; this is a non-lexical scene of night enveloping a person, like the section’s night as an entered garment.
Daylight is stripped from night, leaving people in darkness; this gives the night/day pair a clothing-removal image complementary to night as covering.
The command to take one’s adornment at every place of prayer brings clothing into a setting of worship, a specific counterpoint to adornment carried as worldly display.
This neighbour to 7:31 asks who forbade God’s adornment and good provisions; it clarifies that adornment can be a divine provision even while the section questions reliance on it.
Horses, mules and donkeys are given for riding and as adornment (وَزِينَةً), making the section’s broad dictionary gloss of adornment concrete in worldly possessions.
People extract ornaments from the sea “which you wear” (حِلْيَةً تَلْبَسُونَهَا), a direct instance of beauty literally carried on the body.
Those who take protectors besides God are compared to a spider taking a house, the weakest of houses; the ayah pictures a shelter that cannot perform the protection the section assigns to taqwa.
Whoever has taqwa is given a way out (يَجْعَل لَّهُ مَخْرَجًا), a specific result of the inner safeguard that parallels the section’s promise of ease.
The opening ayah says rivalry in abundance distracts people; 102:2 names the grave as its endpoint, exposing the impermanence behind wealth as ornament.

The source section’s dictionary branch gives debt as a secondary sense of ridā; this ayah treats a debt as a specified obligation to be recorded, so the link is that secondary debt-as-mantle sense, not a Quranic garment image.
